title: "Vector Database"
description: "A database that stores vector representations and supports similarity-oriented retrieval."
term: "Vector Database"
letter: "V"
category: "Retrieval"
difficulty: "Intermediate"

## Simple explanation

A vector database stores numeric representations of items and helps find items
whose vectors are similar to a query vector. It is often used to retrieve
relevant text passages, images, or products.

## Technical explanation

Vector databases store vectors with identifiers and often metadata. A query
vector is compared with stored vectors using a selected distance or similarity
function. For large collections, approximate nearest-neighbor indexes trade
some recall for lower latency and resource use. Filtering, updates, metadata
semantics, and index configuration affect results as much as the similarity
metric.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Similarity search is a common retrieval component in recommendation, semantic
search, and retrieval-augmented generation. A database can provide persistence,
indexing, filtering, and operational interfaces, but it does not decide what a
useful embedding or retrieval policy is.

## How it works

Encode source items into vectors, store each vector with an ID and any
retrieval metadata, and encode each query using the compatible encoder. Search
the index for nearest candidates, apply filters or reranking if needed, and
return the associated records.

## Practical example

For a documentation search system, split documents into passages, embed them,
and store the vectors with source URLs and access-control metadata. At query
time, retrieve similar passages and verify that filtering and permissions are
applied before returning content.

## Common misconceptions

- A vector database does not guarantee semantic relevance; that depends on
  embeddings, chunking, metrics, filters, and evaluation.
- Similarity is not truth or authority. Retrieved results still need suitable
  ranking and downstream handling.
